standard.title: Create geographical descriptions, explanations and responses
standard.description: create descriptions, explanations and responses, using geographical knowledge and geographical tools as appropriate, and concepts and terms that incorporate and acknowledge research findings
standard.prior_knowledge: At Y9, students created descriptions, explanations and responses using geographical knowledge, tools, concepts and terms (AC9HG9S06). At Y10 the same descriptor applies with added complexity: explicit use of tone appropriate to purpose and audience (including authoritative tone), formal use of structural features, and integration of geospatial data representations as part of the response.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students create descriptions, explanations and responses that use appropriate structural features, incorporate geographical knowledge and tools, deploy concepts and terms accurately, acknowledge research findings, and apply tone appropriate to purpose and audience.

nodes.label: Structural features and purposeful organisation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can create a description or explanation for a purpose using structural features to organise ideas, findings, impacts and actions.
nodes.minimum_width: Produce a structured written response with at least two identifiable structural features (e.g. sub-headings, introduction, body, conclusion) that organise the content for its purpose.
nodes.typical_width: Create a description for a specific purpose using structural features — sub-headings, logical sequencing, topic sentences — to organise ideas, findings, impacts and actions; align the structure to the purpose and audience.
wider: Evaluate the structural choices in a model geographical response — explaining why certain structural features serve the purpose and audience of that text

Produce two versions of the same content using different structural approaches for different audiences (e.g. a formal report for a government audience vs a community information document) and explain the structural differences
Analyse how geospatial data representations (maps, graphs, tables) are integrated into the structure of a response to support the argument, not just illustrate it

response_modes.reason: Structural choices are audience and purpose dependent — students benefit from practising structures for different text types (report, explanation, proposal, description) to build flexible writing repertoire.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Writing for different purposes and audiences with different structural conventions is a core transferable literacy. Exposure to multiple text types — report, explanation, proposal — builds a more flexible and purposeful writing capability.
success_criteria: Students produce a response with at least two structural features that support the organisation of ideas for the stated purpose
Students explain how the structural choices they made support the reader's understanding

nodes.label: Incorporating geographical knowledge, tools and concepts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can present conclusions using geospatial technologies and digital tools, incorporating geographical knowledge, concepts and terms that reflect and acknowledge research findings.
nodes.minimum_width: Include at least one geospatial or digital tool output as part of a response, and use at least two geographical concepts or terms accurately, with acknowledgement of research sources.
nodes.typical_width: Present conclusions using geospatial technologies and digital tools (e.g. HDI trend graphs, wellbeing maps, GIS outputs); use geographical concepts and terms accurately and consistently; acknowledge research findings that support each major claim.
wider: Create a response that integrates multiple data representations (map, graph, table) into a coherent argument — explaining what each representation contributes to the overall explanation
Evaluate the data representations in a published geographical report for their accuracy, relevance and argumentative function, then produce an improved version
Produce a response where geospatial data visualisations are specifically designed to reveal a spatial relationship or trend that supports the central claim

response_modes.reason: Building a repertoire of geospatial and digital tool outputs that students can accurately incorporate in responses requires practice across multiple tool types — each tool type has conventions for integration into written responses.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Tool integration into written responses is a distinct skill from tool use alone — students who have practised integrating multiple representation types develop a more sophisticated geographical communication capability.
success_criteria: Students incorporate at least one geospatial or digital tool output accurately into a response, explaining what it shows
Students use at least two geographical concepts or terms accurately and acknowledge research findings that support their claims

nodes.label: Applying tone appropriate to purpose and audience
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop an explanation using an authoritative tone appropriate to purpose and audience, referring to data representations and research findings when explaining a strategy or phenomenon.
nodes.minimum_width: Produce a response that demonstrates an identifiable tone choice (e.g. authoritative, persuasive, informative) appropriate to the stated purpose and audience.
nodes.typical_width: Develop an explanation using an authoritative tone, with reference to representations of data and research findings; adjust tone appropriately when explaining strategies to improve sustainability or wellbeing to different audiences; maintain consistency between tone, purpose and content.
wider: Produce the same content with two different tones for two different audiences — evaluating how vocabulary, sentence structure and hedging language shift with audience
Analyse tone in a policy document and a community information text about the same geographical issue, identifying the linguistic features that produce each tone
Evaluate when authoritative tone is and is not appropriate in geographical communication — examining contexts where more provisional or dialogic language is more honest or more effective

response_modes.reason: Tone is the final integrating element of geographical communication — it requires students to coordinate structural choices, concept use, data integration and language register into a coherent text that achieves its communicative purpose. The teaching signal is that tone is not a separate layer added at the end, but a quality that runs through all the decisions made in producing the text.

success_criteria: Students produce a response with an identifiable and consistent tone appropriate to the stated purpose and audience
Students refer to at least one data representation or research finding in their explanation, integrating it into the argument rather than simply appending it
